question: to the Commission Wouter Beke (PPE) Subject:

Yellow nutsedge (Cyperus esculentus) is a growing problem for agriculture in several Member States. It spreads through underground tubers and earthmoving and is particularly difficult to eradicate. Infestations can lead to restrictions on cultivation and significant losses of income. Available plant protection products vary between Member States and generally provide only limited suppression of yellow nutsedge. At the same time, rules on dosage, timing of application, buffer zones, crop rotation and set-aside can make effective integrated pest management more difficult. In addition, where the notification of an infestation automatically leads to severe cultivation restrictions, an undesirable incentive to refrain from notifying infections may arise, thereby encouraging further spread. 1.
Is the Commission aware that yellow nutsedge is a growing problem in several Member States?
Does the Commission intend to launch a study on the need for a coordinated European strategy for the monitoring, notification, prevention and integrated control of yellow nutsedge?

How does it intend to improve zonal authorisation, mutual recognition and the expansion of authorised uses of effective products, whilst maintaining a high level of protection for people and the environment?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.9.2026) The Commission is aware of the spread of yellow nutsedge (Cyperus esculentus) in several Member States where it did originally not naturally occur. However, as its native range appears to include some Member States of the European Union, the species falls outside the scope of EU Regulation 1143/2014 on the prevention and management of the introduction and spread of invasive aliens (the IAS regulation). It was not identified as a priority invasive alien species (IAS) by the 2025 Horizon scanning report on IAS1. A Horizon Europe2 Cluster 63 topic4 on emerging plant pest risks will open early next year for applications. As regards plant protection products (PPP), the Food and Feed Safety Simplification Package adopted by the Commission on 16 December 20255 aims at creating a regulatory system which is more agile and effective and can ensure a more rapid response to emerging issues while remaining equally protective as the current system. As part of the Package, the Commission proposed enhanced provisions on mutual recognition of PPP authorisations. such as opening the possibility for a wider group of stakeholders to apply, and simplified requirements for minor-use extensions. To ensure that farmers have access to essential PPP for which alternatives are not available, several other specific amendments were also proposed. These measures include, among others, the approvals of active substances unlimited in time in some cases, enhanced approval for a limited period of certain substances to control serious danger to plant production, simplified data protection.
